newsitem.title: CANADA: WTO rules against Canada on U.S. magazines.
newsitem.headline: WTO rules against Canada on U.S. magazines.

text.p: The World Trade Organization has ruled against Canada's attempt to protect its magazine industry from U.S. competition by taxing Canadian editions of U.S. magazines, Canadian newspapers reported on Friday.

The Globe and Mail and Financial Post newspapers said a confidential WTO decision, communicated to Ottawa and Washington on Thursday, strruck down other Canadian protectionist policies such as preferential postal rates and tariff restrictions on magazines.
"We lost," the Globe and Mail quoted a Canadian official as saying.
Canadian International Trade Department spokesman Charles Larabie effectively confirmed the WTO panel ruling, but gave no details and said Canada was considering its options.

"We are still considering the report, and whether or not we are going to seek clarification or make an appeal remains to be seen," Larabie told Reuters. "There is still another month to go before thee final report comes out."
"We'll be working very closely with the magazine industry to try and assess what we are going to do," he said.
The Canadian newspaper reports said Ottawa would have a chance to change the three-member WTO panel's ruling before a final judgment in February.
The dispute began in December 1995 when Ottawa imposed an 80 percent tax on advertising in U.S. magazines that published editions in Canada.
The tax hit the Canadian edition of Sports Illustrated, owned by Time Warner Inc.. And in March 1996, the U.S. government took Waashington's challenge of the controversial tax to the WTO.

Despite Canadian laws dating back to 1965 protecting Canada's publishing induustry, about 70 to 90 percent of Canada's cultural industry is dominated by U.S. films and publications, according to International Trade Minister Art Eggleton.

"To us this is a matter of culture. And it's a small piece of our cultural identity in the magazine industry that we are trying to preserve by this law on split-run magazines," Eggleton told Reuters in an interview last year.
Canada does not allow income tax deductions to Canadians who advertise in Canadian editions of U.S. magazines and postage rates for such publications are higher than rates for Canadian magazines.
